Assertion acceptance, source balances and transferable claims
30 September 2026. Source-level analysis supporting the coordinated pDAI proposal.
What can be proved
For the reviewed historical Nitro implementation, an assertion that passes the parent contract's
admission and confirmation predicates can be confirmed without the parent re-executing its claimed L2
computation. If the assertion is invalid and no effective honest challenge prevents confirmation, the
parent can accept an incorrect execution result. Its associated message root can then become an
accepted Outbox root. This is a concrete consequence of optimistic verification.
The proposition has two independent premises: the ordinary contract predicates are satisfied, and no
effective challenge or other intervention blocks acceptance. The absence of a challenge alone does not
satisfy staking, ancestry, inbox, deadline or pause checks. A rival live stake can prevent confirmation
even before a fraud-proof game finishes. Conversely, the mere existence of challenge code does not
ensure that someone will use it successfully and in time.
This is stronger than saying validator control is irrelevant. It is narrower than saying validator keys confer
unrestricted mint authority over every L1 token. Incorrect message acceptance can compromise a
gateway's assumptions; the gateway still executes its own destination code.
Reproduction baseline
The historical cutoff is Ethereum block 17,232,999, 10 May 2023 at 22:36:11 UTC. The reviewed Nitro
source is commit 3d90a211ff1a0b0bb3fcebe103d3d375b636a211, before that cutoff. It is an upstream code
baseline, not a bytecode-equivalence certificate for every PulseChain proxy implementation at every
later block. It does not import modern BoLD behavior into a 2023 fork. The earlier historical bridge study
(Appendix 13) records the cutoff and repository selection.
The release preserves eight downloaded source documents and their SHA-256 hashes in artifacts/
pulsechain-coordinated-mechanism-20260930/sources/manifest.json. The current Nitro white paper is supporting
architectural documentation; the pinned contracts determine the historical function analysis.

Primary sources: RollupUserLogic, RollupCore, RollupLib, Outbox, L1ArbitrumGateway.
The decisive logical distinction is commitment versus correctness. A consistent hash commits the
asserter to a claim. It does not establish that the claim follows from valid execution. Optimistic fraud-
proof participation supplies that missing check. If this defense fails, a well-formed false claim may
survive. The Nitro white paper, sections 1.1, 2.2 and 5–6, states the honest-participant assumption and
separates deterministic execution from confirmation to the parent chain.
Why impossibility of challenge is not established
The same pinned RollupUserLogic contains two public functions that can disable the validator whitelist: 
removeWhitelistAfterFork checks a chain-ID change against the implementation's immutable deployment
chain ID; removeWhitelistAfterValidatorAfk checks elapsed inactivity. The latter uses the latest node creation
block, the confirmation period and an additional 45,818 blocks. Block counts must not be converted to
PulseChain time using an Ethereum block-time assumption.
pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 150

If an inherited implementation retains an Ethereum deployment chain ID and the fork changes 
block.chainid, the fork predicate can matter directly. A current implementation replacement, proxy routing
or different deployed version can change this assessment. No state-changing call was made in this study.
Therefore a proof that PulseChain challenges are impossible needs the deployed implementation and
routing at the chosen block, actual whitelist state, applicable escape functions, challenge dependencies,
staking access and transaction inclusion conditions. A quiet validator set, unavailable public RPC or
absence of observed disputes does not settle those questions. This study proves the conditional
acceptance mechanism, not permanent exclusive control in deployment.
Four capabilities, not one
Claiming a result: an operator can submit a claimed L2 result if admitted.
Having the parent accept it: the confirmation and challenge conditions apply.
Using a source balance in applications: valid execution requires token permissions, or a
separately assumed modified source execution environment. Honest Nitro nodes deterministically
computing the original rules do not acquire spendable balances merely because an incorrect parent
assertion won.
Receiving a destination asset: an accepted message still reaches a particular receiver whose
code determines transfers, minting, limits and failures.
An accepted false message root is economically consequential even without an honest source
application recognizing the claimed transaction. It should be described as a failure of the message-
authentication assumption, not proof that ordinary source lending, staking and token issuance all
executed successfully. The proposal may instead assume valid authorized source issuance and
compatible receipts; that route does not depend on a false assertion.
ERC20, vault shares and NFTs
ERC20 assets can be bridged through suitable contracts. The historical 
L1ReverseCustomGateway.inboundEscrowTransfer calls bridgeMint on its mapped destination token. That is a
concrete source-native representation mechanism, not a universal minter for arbitrary tokens already
held by Curve pools. The function bodies establish direction; a contradictory comment in this source
must not override them. Pinned reverse gateway.
A vault or staking receipt can represent assets that remain invested on the source chain. Many such
shares are ERC20s: ERC-4626 standardizes tokenized vault shares using that interface. A position can
instead be represented by an ERC-721 NFT or an ERC-1155 claim when the application defines the
entitlement and a compatible bridge preserves exclusive ownership. NFT metadata alone does not
enforce custody, withdrawal or cross-chain redemption.

pDAI stabilization thesis · 4 October 2026 151

An NFT cannot be passed directly as the input coin of an ordinary fungible Curve pool. A buyer, lender,
authorized redemption mechanism or fungible adapter must convert its economic entitlement into the
exact accepted input token. Fractionalizing a position changes its interface, not the underlying assets or
their withdrawal limits. The owner cannot sell an exclusive receipt and also count its underlying as freely
available collateral elsewhere.
Section 3.2.5 of the Nitro white paper explicitly discusses NFT bridging and source-native tokens as
possible bridge extensions. It does not specify a deployed pARB–PulseChain NFT liquid-staking
integration. No such complete route has been established by this evidence set. Architectural support is
documented; the particular contracts, ownership, custody and funded conversion are the remaining
implementation evidence.
Application to the thesis
The strongest defensible proposal grants coordinated source operation, extensive issuance capacity and
compatible destination acceptance, then traces the assets received and sold. Trillions of nominal source
units can be an assumed input without assigning those units a dollar value. The capability argument
explains why accepted claims could reach destination markets. The network experiment (Appendix 31)
tests what renewed accepted inputs do to those markets after arrival.
Common beneficial ownership, ecosystem-aligned incentives and sustained cooperation remain explicit
scenario premises where not evidenced. Neither arbitrary assertion capacity nor an NFT interface proves
those premises.
